tip: Hindi 'until' carries a built-in not: जब तक अंजलि नहीं आती (jab tak Anjali nahin aati) is literally 'as long as Anjali doesn't come'. English has no negative there – Hindi requires the नहीं.
The if-clause looks past: ठीक रही (theek rahi = stayed fine) even though it's about tomorrow. Hindi often uses a past form after अगर (agar = if) for future conditions.
Hindi relatives lead: जो चाबी मेज़ पर है, वह (jo chaabi mez par hai, vah) = 'which key is on the table, that one'. The जो clause comes first, then वह picks it up – reversed from English.
No tense shift in reported speech: कहा कि वह जल्दी आएगी (kaha ki vah jaldi aayegi) = 'said that she WILL come soon'. Hindi keeps the original future where English backshifts to 'would'.
जैसे ही ट्रेन आए (jaise hi train aae): the short आए signals the train hasn't come yet. Awaited events in time clauses take this form – not आती है (aati hai = comes) or आएगी (aayegi = will come).
दूध ले आना (doodh le aana) looks like 'to bring milk' but works as a command for later: bring it when you go. The -ना form is Hindi's gentle do-it-later imperative.
चाहे कुछ भी हो (chaahe kuchh bhi ho) = 'no matter what', literally 'whether anything even be'. चाहे plus the bare हो covers every possibility at once.
